# A graph that grows itself: what a knowledge graph is worth when nobody is there to query it

*Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Abstract

Ultrastable R&D (Ultrastable): The common view is that a knowledge graph is a search aid: you build it, then someone queries it. Microsoft's GraphRAG work (Edge and others, 2024) showed graphs help most on questions about a whole corpus, by grouping entities into communities and summarising each one. LightRAG and HippoRAG pushed the same idea toward cheaper, incremental updates. Link prediction and Swanson's old literature-based discovery go further: the useful output is the missing edge. Ashby's ultrastable system needs exactly that kind of signal, a measure that tells the second loop when the first one is stuck. So we built the graph into every system Ultrastable runs. Each tick reads only rows past a cursor, pulls out ids, rule tags and file paths without a model, then has a small model name the entities and relations in those new rows, embeds them, and summarizes each community whose members changed. The spend throttle slows this down; it never switches it off. A pair that reads alike, has no edge and shares no neighbour becomes a lead. Two leads a day at most become work items. A lead counts as kept only when a later change links the pair for real. Most graph work assumes a person asks a question and the graph helps answer it. We test the other use: a system that builds the graph from everything it writes down, looks for pairs that read alike but are not linked, files each one as work, and counts how many turn out to be real. 1 of 1 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## 1. Introduction

A common view holds that a knowledge graph is a search index: it only pays off when a person asks it something. This paper tests a different account: a graph that is rebuilt from every record and mined for missing links produces its own work, and whether that work was worth doing can be counted.

Most graph work assumes a person asks a question and the graph helps answer it. We test the other use: a system that builds the graph from everything it writes down, looks for pairs that read alike but are not linked, files each one as work, and counts how many turn out to be real.

The question is narrow and testable. For each of 1 findings we name the concern, the mechanism in this system that is meant to answer it, and a metric from the system's own records that can show the answer does not hold. The findings cover systems.

## 2. Background and related work

The common view is that a knowledge graph is a search aid: you build it, then someone queries it. Microsoft's GraphRAG work (Edge and others, 2024) showed graphs help most on questions about a whole corpus, by grouping entities into communities and summarising each one. LightRAG and HippoRAG pushed the same idea toward cheaper, incremental updates. Link prediction and Swanson's old literature-based discovery go further: the useful output is the missing edge. Each tick reads only rows past a cursor, pulls out ids, rule tags and file paths without a model, then has a small model name the entities and relations in those new rows, embeds them, and summarizes each community whose members changed. The spend throttle slows this down; it never switches it off. A pair that reads alike, has no edge and shares no neighbour becomes a lead. Two leads a day at most become work items. A lead counts as kept only when a later change links the pair for real. [2]

Evidence base: The core knowledge graph this system rebuilds every day from its own work items, studies and rules (ops/kgraph), and the leads it files and settles (ops/kgraph/leads.jsonl).

The design under test takes its name and its central mechanism from Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first feedback loop that acts on the world, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters only when an essential variable leaves its limits.

Ultrastable is that design as code [2]. Its loops, limits and ledgers are public, so each claim below can be checked against the files named.

## 3. Method

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history. Reproduce with `python3 -m foundation research --report`; every finding not met has a Q-RES item whose closing probe is `python3 -m foundation research --probe STUDY:F`.

Each finding is stated as a target on one metric, with a prediction logged before the measurement. A finding is met only when the measured value meets the target; a metric with no readings is reported as not measured, never as met.

## 5. Discussion

K1. The graph keeps itself current. Every system Ultrastable runs keeps a knowledge graph of its own data, built and refreshed by its own tick, with no setup. [2] In this system the answer is KGRAPH-1 (the daily build reads every work item, study and rule, and a probe fails when the graph is over 36 hours old); KGRAPH-1 (each tick Worker reads only rows past its cursor and files KG-LAG when it falls behind). The metric, share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending, reads 1.0 (n = 5) against a target of >= 1. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

## 6. Limitations

- Extraction. Every tick Worker now asks a small Workers AI model to name the entities and relations in its new rows, a few records per call, and embeds them in one batched call. The repository half that builds the core graph in CI still extracts ids, tags, paths and terms only.
- Communities. Communities come from label propagation, not the Leiden clustering GraphRAG uses, and only communities whose membership changed are summarized again. The model's summaries are proposals and are not checked against the records yet.
- Cost. AI work is scaled by the account's spend level and capped at a share of the included daily allocation; the neuron counts are estimates per call, recorded per system per day, not a meter reading.
- Yield is young. A lead needs days to be acted on, so the kept share starts near zero and only means something after a few weeks of filings.

## 7. Conclusion

On this system's records, 1 of 1 findings hold. No finding is open.

That is evidence against the view that a graph only helps when someone queries it: the properties tested here are engineering properties of the loop, and each can be measured and repaired without waiting on a better model.
